craft_claim: The confessional mode draws its force from performed self-accusation addressed to a witness, treating disclosure as a truth-producing act rather than a neutral description.

supporting_evidence.location: Confessions, books I-IX; the narrated life addressed to God and overheard by the reader
supporting_evidence.note: Augustine turns the narrating self into an object of examination, disclosing fault and motive to a witness; this establishes the addressed-disclosure convention.

supporting_evidence.location: Part Three, 'Scientia Sexualis', on confession as a technology of truth
supporting_evidence.note: Confession is described as a ritual of discourse that produces a truth about the self within a power relation between speaker and interlocutor.

supporting_evidence.location: Introduction and readings of Rousseau and Dostoevsky
supporting_evidence.note: Brooks argues Western culture treats confessional speech as a prime measure of authenticity while simultaneously suspecting it of being coerced or self-serving.

counterevidence.note: Confessional truth is systematically unreliable; the mode promises authenticity it cannot guarantee, which is itself a reproducible failure mode.

scope: Memoir, personal essay, and first-person fiction that performs self-accusation or exposure.
exceptions: Non-Western and devotional traditions may frame intimate address as devotion rather than guilt; see clm-tone-intimate-crosscultural-norms.
